meta.title: RetailCo Store Performance Operating System
meta.subtitle: Closing the gap between your best and worst stores across APAC

slides.title: RetailCo Store Performance Operating System
slides.subtitle: One joined-up proposal to see, hear, bottle, and scale what works
slides.script: We are not going to pitch four separate tools to RetailCo. We are going to pitch one operating system for store performance. The starting point is simple: somewhere in the estate, a best store is already doing the right things, and somewhere else, a worst store is missing them. Our job is to close that gap deliberately, not by waiting for Monday spreadsheets or hoping the right manager is on shift, but by making the shop floor observable, coachable, searchable, and repeatable across 120 stores.

slides.quote: I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor. I get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week.
slides.script: We should start exactly where the COO started. The issue is not that RetailCo lacks effort, or data, or managers who care. The issue is timing and distance. By the time the spreadsheet arrives on Monday, the moment that mattered has already passed: the missed greeting, the poor conversion conversation, the queue that formed, the new hire who copied the wrong habit. Spacesight and Echo change that operating rhythm by turning the floor and the customer conversation into live signals, not late summaries.

slides.title: 120 stores cannot be managed through one Monday spreadsheet
slides.label: APAC stores
slides.note: The operating system has to reveal store reality while there is still time to act.
slides.script: At 120 stores, leadership cannot learn store reality by walking every floor, and store managers cannot all be coached one by one from headquarters. Spacesight gives us the visual layer: what is happening in store, where friction appears, and which execution patterns separate strong stores from weaker ones. Echo gives us the conversational layer: what staff actually say to customers and how those conversations are scored. Joined together, they make the best store and the worst store comparable through the same lens.

slides.title: The gap is already quantified
slides.script: RetailCo has already given us the three numbers that define the performance gap. The best managers outsell the worst ones by 3x. A new hire takes six weeks to become productive, and that journey depends on whoever happens to be working that day. And leadership sees last week on Monday. Our proposal is built around compressing those gaps. Not by inventing a new management philosophy, but by capturing what the best store does, converting it into a repeatable operating model, and pushing that model into daily work.

slides.title: One operating system, not four disconnected tools

rows.right: Spacesight shows what is happening across the shop floor.
Echo captures and scores frontline customer conversations.
Harbor Wiki bottles manager methods into searchable guidance.
Alivia packages the system into a coherent client proposal.
Open item: use store signals to brief scheduling decisions.

slides.script: The value is in the joins. Spacesight sees the floor, Echo hears the interaction, Harbor Wiki turns what works into shared operating knowledge, and Alivia packages that into one proposal we can align around. Scheduling is the one pain we should treat honestly. None of these products is a dedicated roster optimizer. What we can do is give scheduling teams better evidence from store reality: where coverage pressure appears, which shifts need stronger coaching, and which operating patterns should inform roster conversations.

slides.title: The best store is already writing the playbook
slides.label: Performance spread between managers
slides.note: The goal is to make the best manager's behaviours visible and reusable.
slides.script: The 3x gap tells us the answer is not theoretical. RetailCo already has managers who know how to sell, coach, recover a conversation, handle traffic, and keep the store moving. The problem is that their methods are trapped in their store and in their heads. Echo helps identify what strong managers and staff actually say. Spacesight shows the floor patterns around that performance. Harbor Wiki then turns those behaviours into a playbook that another store can search, learn, and apply.

slides.label: A closed loop from signal to coaching to standard practice
slides.script: This is why we should avoid a tool-by-tool purchase decision. If RetailCo buys Spacesight alone, it can see more. If it buys Echo alone, it can hear more. If it buys Harbor Wiki alone, it can document more. But the operating system is different: it observes, interprets, and standardises. The best store becomes the reference model. The worst store gets specific coaching based on its own reality. Headquarters stops asking for anecdotes and starts managing from the same evidence base as the store teams.

slides.title: Six weeks of onboarding should not depend on the shift lottery
slides.label: Current onboarding period
slides.note: Harbor Wiki makes the best available guidance independent of who is on duty.
slides.script: Onboarding is where the performance gap reproduces itself. If a new hire learns from a strong manager, they inherit stronger habits. If they learn from a weaker shift, they inherit weaker ones. Harbor Wiki breaks that dependency by becoming the store’s source of truth for how RetailCo wants work done. Echo can feed examples of strong customer language. Spacesight can highlight execution patterns worth teaching. So the new hire is no longer limited to whoever happens to be working that day.

slides.title: Close the gap between Store A and Store B

rows.right: Echo scores calls and surfaces coachable moments.
Spacesight exposes missed actions while they matter.
Harbor Wiki turns habits into searchable guidance.
Alivia frames the system as one operating model.
Open scheduling item informed by store signals.

slides.script: We can now make the contrast concrete. Store A, the best store, has better conversations, cleaner execution, and manager habits worth copying. Store B, the weaker store, does not need generic encouragement. It needs specific evidence and specific next actions. Echo tells us which conversations need coaching. Spacesight tells us which floor moments are breaking. Harbor Wiki gives staff the proven answer. Alivia helps us package this as one change programme, while scheduling remains an adjacent workstream that benefits from the new evidence.

slides.title: One success metric for the first review
slides.label: Metric: narrow the 3x manager performance gap
slides.script: For the first review, we should resist measuring everything. The single success metric should be whether we are narrowing the 3x gap between the best and worst store managers. That keeps the operating system honest. Spacesight and Echo should expose the behaviours behind the gap. Harbor Wiki should translate those behaviours into repeatable guidance. Store teams should be able to act before the next Monday spreadsheet. We propose reviewing that metric with RetailCo on 30 November 2026, with the scheduling item tracked separately.

slides.title: Our ask: commit to one operating system
slides.subtitle: Use the best store to lift the worst store, then scale across 120 stores.
bullets: Confirm the 3x gap as the success metric
Select pilot stores representing best and worst performance
Stand up Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki together
slides.script: The decision we are asking RetailCo to make is not which tool to trial first. We are asking RetailCo to commit to the operating system logic: see the floor with Spacesight, hear the conversation with Echo, bottle the best practice in Harbor Wiki, and package the change through Alivia. We start with the contrast between the best and worst stores, because that is where the business case already exists. Then we review one metric on one date: whether the 3x manager performance gap is closing.

approach.angle: Frame it as one operating system rather than four tools. The products are worth more joined up than bought separately, and that is the whole pitch.
approach.device: Contrast two stores - the best and the worst - and close the gap between them on stage.
approach.opener: Open on the customer's own words - put their quote on screen before anything else.
approach.close: Close by proposing a single success metric and the date you would review it against.

structure.label: side titles, one big number a page
structure.brief: Built out of NUMBERS. Most slides lead with a single figure taken from the scenario and explain what it costs. Use "bignum" at least four times. Never invent a figure you were not given.
